# Field Guide: Preparing a Home for a 72-Hour Power Outage

This guide prepares an ordinary household to manage safely and comfortably through a power outage of up to seventy-two hours. It assumes a temperate climate and no backup generator. Work through the sections in order; earlier sections cover the preparations that matter most.

## Water

Store four litres of water per person per day, twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours. Half is for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene. Use food-grade containers, keep them out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months. Given advance warning of a storm, also fill the bathtub; bathtub water is for flushing toilets and washing, never drinking.

## Food

Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food for three days: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk. Choose foods that need no cooking, and own a manual can opener, since an electric one will be useless. Eat perishable refrigerator food first, then freezer food, and only then the emergency shelf.

## Refrigerator and freezer

An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about four hours. A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about forty-eight hours, but a half-full one for only about twenty-four, so keep the freezer consolidated and full, even with containers of frozen water. Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a reminder note to each. Discard any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius; when in doubt, throw it out.

## Light

Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light, and avoid candles entirely, since they are a leading cause of house fires during outages. Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each. Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, placed where they can be found in the dark.

## Heat and safety

Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window: each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal. Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on every floor where people sleep. In cold weather, gather everyone in one small room on the home's south-facing side and close the door; layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater. If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot stay warm, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.

## Communication and information

Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and learn your local emergency station's frequency before the outage. Charge every phone and power bank whenever a storm is forecast; a full twenty-thousand-milliamp-hour power bank recharges a typical phone roughly four times. Put your phone in low-power mode at the outage's start, and agree in advance on one out-of-area contact whom every household member will text, since texts cross congested networks more reliably than voice calls.

## Medical needs

Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, rotating them to stay in date. Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally stays usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist beforehand. Write your pharmacy, doctor, and poison-control numbers on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.

## When the power returns

Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, letting the grid stabilise. Check the freezer: food still holding ice crystals can be safely refrozen. Restock everything used within one week, starting with water and batteries. Finally, write a one-page note on what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one gap before the next outage.
hardConstraintNote: Still a fully self-contained instruction document: all nine section headers remain (Water, Food, Refrigerator and freezer, Light, Heat and safety, Communication and information, Medical needs, When the power returns) plus the intro framing (72-hour horizon, temperate climate, no generator, work in order). Every actionable quantity, item, threshold, ordered sequence, and its reason is present in the text itself, with no external reference, table, or omitted step. A reader holding only this text can execute the entire preparation exactly as the original instructs.
killedLeverCitations: none — notes/KILLED_LEVERS.md has no filed K-ids (table empty); nothing to avoid re-proposing
rationale: The guide is already fact-dense, so gains come from rhetorical tails and redundant re-statements, not from cutting content. I made one sentence-level pass across all nine sections: (1) removed throat-clearing openers ('This guide explains how to prepare an ordinary household to manage...' -> 'This guide prepares an ordinary household to manage...'); (2) converted narrative connective tissue to appositive lists (the food and medication choices collapse into a single colon-led list without losing an item); (3) turned passive/periphrastic constructions active ('should be discarded' -> 'Discard', 'If a storm is forecast and you have advance warning' -> 'Given advance warning of a storm'); (4) fused duplicated nouns ('twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours' kept once, 'the other half covers' -> 'half for'). NO fact was deleted: every number (4 L/day, 12 L, 6 months, 4 h fridge, 48 h / 24 h freezer, 2 h above 4 C, 1 light/person + 2 spare battery sets, 10 C, 20000 mAh ~4 recharges, 7-day meds, 28 days insulin, 5 min, 1 week), every listed item, every causal reason (candles->fires, CO->fatal, texts->congested networks, dead phone->phone book, ice crystals->refreezable), and every ordered step survives. Structure and all headers stay intact, so gate risk is low. Measured against baseline 730 (frontier.json), this reaches ~627 tokens, just under the family's realistic reach and well inside the line-editor cost band.
title: Single line-editor tightening pass: cut filler, activate passives, fuse redundant restatements
